items.title: Bob Magnusson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999
items.q: Yeah I love working with Roger Kellaway and John Guerin. We’ve been trying to do something as a trio.

ctx.x: Roger Kellaway — I should tell my film audience.

Yeah I love working with Roger Kellaway and John Guerin. We’ve been trying to do something as a trio. It’s kind of hard to get anybody to — we’ve made a CD but we haven’t been able to get anybody to buy it. Roger does — he’s such a versatile musician. He’s done film writing and composed concertos for orchestras, and you name it and he’s done it. And he has this terrific spirit of adventure when he plays, like you were bringing out. And so I really have to pay attention. It can go any place at any time with Roger.

items.title: Roger Kellaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: you and Bob Magnusson just basically started playing

ctx.x: That’s right. And the reason that I decided on that particular category for myself is because the idea of what a jazz pianist does is too limiting. I’ve listened to much too much twentieth century classical music, which is the necessary ingredient for your understanding how it is I play and how I think, for me to just think of myself as a jazz pianist, because there’s too much Webern and Alban Berg and Prokofiev and Stravinsky, and onward to Stockhausen and Messiaen and more modern composers that have shaped my…

When you play, for instance I’ll use last night as an example, I heard you play “All Blues.” It was very interesting because we weren’t sure what the tune was going to be, and you started playing, you and Bob Magnusson just basically started playing. Do you have an idea before your hands hit the keyboard, as where that’s going, that introduction?
No. Well the answer is yes and no. Because we had never played that tune that way. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
